what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Five agent readers make long articles easier to consume
sections.para: The articles are deep and long, so rather than shorten them, five agent readers go through each after it is written: a Librarian, a Cartographer, a Historian, an Explainer and a Storyteller. On five agent behaviour policy articles they catalogued 662 items, flagged 32 problems, mapped 45 concepts and produced nine maps and five decks.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Prose first, then five readers extract views from it
sections.para: The article stays the source and no reader adds a claim: two readers build a graph, three write short views. The run checked 662 anchors verbatim and flagged 32 problems, acting as fact-checkers unasked. New concepts across the five fell 17, 11, 5, 11, 1, and each article now opens with Read it another way.

sections.label: Why the prose comes first
sections.line: Writing finds the argument, so the graph comes after
sections.para: Generating an article from a graph does not work, because writing is how a journalist discovers the narrative, as Liquid content needs water said. That article also imagined a historian and a librarian for each story, and projections checked against one graph. This applies the idea to the site's own articles without changing how they are written.

sections.label: Five readers
sections.line: Two readers build the graph, three write for people
sections.para: The roles come from the SG/Send agent team. The Librarian catalogues every item with its source sentence; the Cartographer, merged with the ontologist, builds three altitudes and maps. The Historian writes under 400 words, the Explainer under 250, and the Storyteller a deck of 6 to 9 slides.

sections.label: The simulation
sections.line: Seven agent runs read five articles in parallel
sections.para: Five articles on agent behaviour policies, from 7 to 10 October, were read by agents each given one role file. Five Librarians ran in parallel using 403,000 tokens, the Cartographer took 14 minutes and 264,000 tokens, and every output was checked against its format by script.

sections.label: What the Librarian found
sections.line: Cataloguing every sentence turned the Librarian into a fact-checker
sections.para: All 662 anchors were found verbatim, with 161 claims against 40 items presented as evidence. Told to flag, not fix, the Librarian raised 32 flags: a 17.8 million total that should be about 14.2 million, a twelve-item list with ten, an unsupported military attribution, content only in images. Corrections will follow separately.

sections.label: What the Cartographer built
sections.line: The Cartographer merged five names for one method
sections.para: It built 13 classes, 24 verbs, 45 concepts and 78 edges at site, topic and article altitude. It merged hope with expectation, second reader with maker-checker, and found one method under five names, moving a rule to a stronger barrier, while keeping reach and blast radius apart. Its 37 feedback items await a second pass.

sections.label: What the Historian found
sections.para: The Historian picked a quoted nugget per article and found the set moved from vocabulary to configuration; Re-anchoring introduced one concept and reused 25. Its unnamed pattern: the rule moves out of the agent, and each article stops one barrier short. It also spotted that new meant new to the set, not the site.

sections.label: The Explainer and the Storyteller
sections.line: Two-minute explanations and code-drawn decks for phones
sections.para: The Explainer writes for a small-business owner: the point, an example, why it matters, one line to remember, defined terms. The Storyteller writes decks as data in nine layouts, rendered at 1080 by 1350 for LinkedIn. Image-model prompts are ready in the vault but unrun, lacking an API key.

sections.label: What it looks like on the page
sections.line: Each article now opens with Read it another way
sections.para: Under the abstract, In two minutes is open by default, with the arc, pictures, map and catalogue a click away; it works without JavaScript and in the markdown twins. The Article Views vault holds role files, catalogues, ontology, maps, decks and checks, and opens as an app.

sections.label: What this does not do
sections.line: The views check articles against themselves, not the world
sections.para: Truth of cited facts remains the Journalist's job. Scripts check anchors, edges, limits and quotes, but a subtly unfair summary passes, so the author reads each view. New is relative without the site altitude, the feedback round trip is unapplied, and the run cost about 1.1 million tokens.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.line: Next: desk roles, the round trip, a site ontology
sections.para: The readers join the Historian on the newsroom desk so every new article gets views. The Librarian's second pass and the flagged corrections follow, a site-wide ontology makes new mean new, and one deck goes through an image model with its cost counted. The articles stay long.
